title: What drives passengers' airline choice?
text: To make things clear, we selected only a few airlines. The trends seem to be the same as those previously observed.

title: What drives passengers' airline choice?
text:
Unfortunately, the dataset did not include any information about passengers’ perception of the airline’s evironmental perspective. However, there is a rich literature on the topic.
Most notably, Mayer et al. (2012) investigated air traveller perceptions of different airlines with regard to green image, and how passengers perceive different measures that airlines can introduce to reduce their environmental impact.
It found that images of environmental-friendliness are specific to particular airlines rather than to airline business models. It also shows that there is no evidence that low-cost airlines have a different green image from full-service network airlines, and that it is possible for airlines to differentiate themselves from their competitors based on their environmental image.
Extracted from: Mayer, R., Ryley, T., & Gillingwater, D. (2012). Passenger perceptions of the green image associated with airlines. Journal Of Transport Geography, 22, 179‑186.

title: What drives passengers' airline choice?
text:
In addition to our bibliographic research, we decided to analyze a dataset of roughly 129,000 flight reviews using R software (see methodology tab) to identify the main factors driving airline choice. Although the dataset did not include information on the perceived environmental performance of airlines, it did provide valuable insights into perceptions of price, service, and comfort (each of these criteria was given a score between 0 and 5).










Due to the very high number of airline companies in the dataset, (there are 505 according to R), some of the following graphs do not mean much. It would be more interesting to categorize airlines and take a closer look at their ratings.











































We observe that Asian airline companies are almost consistently rated higher than other European and American companies. However there are any biases: we only selected a few airlines and these are not at all representative of the whole continental sector. American companies generally rank the lowest in our ratings.

This variable “value for money” and “price sensitivity” is measured using the variable ValueRating that was included in the dataset, and which reflects passengers’ subjective balance between the price they paid and the quality of the experience. It does not measure the actual ticket price, but if whether passengers felt the service was worth the cost.

























The plots clearly show things like perceived value decreasing and even plummeting for many airlines, fluctuating service quality, and price/value factors shifting. Several elements present in the literature help explain this. Also, let us not forget that these ratings are SUBJECTIVE which may have important implications for our findings.
To begin with, one of the most important factors that we will focus on is COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath: indeed, a 2024 paper (Kim et al. (2024) has shown that passengers’ expectations and criteria for choosing their airlines have drastically changed, and that service quality perceptions were disrupted by the pandemic (linked to cancellations or staffing shortages).
Research (Yalvaç, 2026) has also shown that the growth and development of online reviews and social media has made passenger experiences far more visible and influential, with the development of online review websites (such as the one we are using in this mini-case study).
Other reasons can also include the deregulation of the industry. Indeed, since airline deregulation (1978 in the US), some airlines have been trying more and more to cut costs to focus on price, which affects how people choose airlines today. During an interview, the Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary has suggested charging for access to toilets and creating standing room at the back of planes.
Batarliene and Slavinskaite (Batarlienė & Slavinskaitė, 2023) suggest that the rise of LCC such as Ryanair or Easy-Jet has changed the expectations of service and quality confort and not only choice criteria, as these companies focus on competitive pricing, which may entail flying to “cheaper” airports or cutting amenities.
This decline affects both low-cost airlines and more premium carriers (see respective sections).

title: What drives passengers' airline choice?
text: This comparison shows that airline choice factors depend strongly on business model: price dominates for low-cost carriers, while service quality and onboard experience are decisive for full-service and premium airlines.

title: 128k Airline Reviews
text:
We resorted to a dataset that was available on Kaggle, a platform for data science and machine learning professionals where we can freely download open data. The data itself was scraped from Airlinequality.com.


This data set was scraped from airlinequality.com and contains text-based reviews in addition to reviewers’ ratings of available dimensions on the website.
The data is available here: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/joelljungstrom/128k-airline-reviews
Extract from the website: “Names of users were purposefully left out from the crawler. Although the earliest review dates back to 2001, note that some dimensions have been added to the website over time. Consequently, not all dimensions have been filled out for each review.”
Screenshot from the actual document:

Because the ticket prices are not observed, we measure price sensitivity using passengers’ value-for-money ratings, which reflect how strongly price influences satisfaction relative to service quality. The dataset also included a column that stipulated whether the trip was business-related or not. Business-related trips were excluded from the analysis.
The variables in this analysis are measured using the passenger-reported ratings. For instance:

Seat comfort is measured using SeatComfortRating
The variables service quality is measured using ServiceRating, which can reflect passengers’ assessments of cabin crew behavior, professionalism, or responsiveness during the flight for instance.
Ground services are measured using GroundServiceRating, which evaluates airport-related processes (i.e. check-in, boarding, and baggage handling etc)
The onboard experience is measured as a composite indicator that combines the FoodRating, EntertainmentRating, and WifiRating

HOWEVER, all variables are subjective evaluations. But, because airline choice is driven by passenger perceptions, these ratings are well suited to analyzing how decision factors have evolved over time.


All data used in the research were obtained from publicly available and ethically sourced secondary datasets. Ethical approval was not required.
